title: Trump Administration Reverses Decades-Old Disability Integration Mandate
summary:
For nearly 50 years, the federal government has said people with disabilities should live, work, and learn in the most integrated setting possible rather than be segregated in institutions like nursing homes. The Trump administration just took its most concrete step yet to reverse that position.

Last week, a federal judge agreed to strip out mentions of 'integration' from federal regulations tied to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a landmark civil rights law that prohibits disability discrimination. The judge did so after the Justice Department declined to defend its own rules in a lawsuit brought by several states challenging the legality of those rules.

Part of what is striking about Texas v. Kennedy is that the federal government was originally the defendant. Then it switched sides and agreed with the states that the integration mandate should be undone.

Bruce Darling, president and CEO of the Center for Disability Rights, said when he heard about the ruling, it felt 'like a knife in your chest.' He said the message people are hearing is that disabled people 'don't have a right to live in freedom, that they can be locked up against their will.'

Jennifer Mathis, a disability rights lawyer at the Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, said the decision removes regulations requiring federally funded programs to provide services in the 'most integrated setting.' She noted the court's decision did not undo integration protections tied to the Americans with Disabilities Act or the landmark Supreme Court decision known as Olmstead. 'My concern is that right now, where we're at is disabled people have a right to integration on paper. It is in the law, but whether it gets practically enforced is a serious question,' Darling said.

The Justice Department did not respond to multiple requests from NPR asking why it is changing course after decades of legal and bipartisan support for community-based services. In 1973, Congress passed Section 504, and advocates fought for years — including a 28-day sit-in in San Francisco in 1977 — to get enforceable regulations.
why_it_matters: The rules about where people with disabilities can live decide whether millions of Americans receive support in their own communities or end up inside institutions — and this case raises a bigger question: what does a right written into law actually mean if the government stops defending it?

background_read: Section 504, part of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, was the first U.S. law to say that discrimination against people with disabilities is illegal. It only applied to programs that receive federal money, so Congress later passed the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) to extend similar protections to private jobs, stores, buses and schools.

In 1999 the Supreme Court decided Olmstead v. L.C., ruling that unjustly keeping people with disabilities in institutions can violate the ADA. Disability rights grew out of the civil rights movement: in 1977, activists occupied federal buildings for weeks — including the 28-day sit-in in San Francisco mentioned in the story — to force the government to finally write rules that could be enforced.

Bruce Darling leads the Center for Disability Rights, a nonprofit run by and for people with disabilities, and Jennifer Mathis works at the Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, a nonprofit that uses the courts to defend the rights of people with mental health conditions.

Texas v. Kennedy is the name of the current lawsuit; the 'v.' stands for versus and separates the two sides in a case. The Justice Department, which did not explain its change of course to NPR, is the federal agency that normally defends the government's rules in court.

perspectives.description: Several states challenged the federal rules as illegal overreach and argued that writing 'integration' into regulation went beyond what Congress authorized. In their view, removing that language restores a proper balance between federal mandates and state flexibility in how services are delivered.

Bruce Darling of the Center for Disability Rights says the ruling felt 'like a knife in your chest' and sends the message that disabled people 'can be locked up against their will'. Jennifer Mathis of the Bazelon Center points out that the regulations requiring federally funded programs to serve people in the 'most integrated setting' are now gone.

For decades, community-based care for people with disabilities enjoyed bipartisan support, rooted in the civil rights era and in the 1973 law that Congress passed and advocates fought to make enforceable. What makes Texas v. Kennedy striking is that the federal government was originally the defendant and then switched to argue against its own rules, leaving courts to settle a question the executive branch normally defends.

The decision did not erase integration protections under the Americans with Disabilities Act or the Supreme Court's Olmstead ruling, so the legal foundation still exists. The open question is enforcement: advocates expect more lawsuits and state-by-state battles, and the Justice Department's silence about why it changed course leaves the long-term direction unclear.
